sweep_summary: Mohawk (moha1258) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (penult; deciding quote is the StressTyp2-style Bonvillain-based text, cite empty; our check store names Hagstrom 1997 as the deciding file we hold). All five title-keyword items are about Mohawk word stress; none has an open full text. Michelson 1981 (HSP 2) is print-only with no online record. Michelson 1983 (two duplicate Glottolog records for one Harvard dissertation) and Michelson 1988 (its published revision, Kluwer, DOI 10.1007/978-94-009-2709-4; paywalled, archive.org borrow-only, HathiTrust search-only) were reached only as Google Books snippets: 1983 §2.4 'Mohawk has preserved the PNI rule of penultimate stress.. made opaque in Mohawk by the operation of epenthesis rules'; 1988 ch.3 'The PLI pattern of penultimate accent and vowel lengthening in accented open penults has been preserved in Mohawk'. Potter 1994 (CLS 30:347-361, print only, not on ROA) snippet: 'stress is penultimate regardless of whether the penult and ultima syllables are open or closed.. Excrescent vowels in penultimate position are not stressed'. Every item confirms the fixed-strict penult coding with epenthetic-vowel invisibility. Best new first-hand statement: Michelson 1988 ch.3 snippet (does not supersede the current source because only a snippet without page was obtained); Michelson 1988 remains the high-priority acquisition. Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, archive.org, HathiTrust, Google Books, ROA and Springer were queried directly. Saved.

new_statements.quote: [sec. 2.4.11] ... stress is obligatory, however. All Mohawk words must contain one and only one stressed vowel. The determination of the placement of stress within the word is complex and will be discussed in detail in 3.7.1. below. Generally, though, stress is placed on the penultimate vowel. Most exceptions to this general rule can be accounted for by subsidiary rules which shift stress from the penultimate to a preceding vowel (see 3.7.2. for the conditions of this adjustment.). [sec. 3.7.21 'Stress'] The problem of the placement of stress within the word is very complex. However, a few patterns can be pointed out here ... To begin with, the preferred syllable to receive stress is the penultimate. A word of more than one syllable spoken in isolation is very rarely stressed on the final syllable. Monosyllabic words are extremely rare. 3.7.22. The rule placing stress on the penultimate syllable must apply before the application of two additional morphophonemic rules. The first such rule supplies epenthetic vowels.

new_statements.relation_note: Same statement as the catalog's fixed-strict penultimate coding and its quote (which is StressTyp2's paraphrase of Bonvillain 1973 p. 47: one stressed vowel per word, usually the penult, epenthesis after stressing yields antepenultimate surface stress, dummy vowel before monosyllables). Adds the rule ordering (stress before e-epenthesis and joiner insertion) and 'very rarely stressed on the final syllable'. Consistent with Michelson 1988 and Potter 1994 held by the project.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Mohawk word has exactly one stressed vowel; stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel; surface exceptions (stress on an earlier vowel, e.g. the antepenult) arise because penultimate stress placement is ordered before two morphophonemic insertion rules (e-epenthesis and the joiner/filler vowel -a-), so inserted vowels can follow the stressed vowel; final stress in polysyllables spoken in isolation is very rare; monosyllables are extremely rare (a prothetic vowel is added to potential monosyllables).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'All Mohawk words must contain one and only one stressed vowel' (sec. 2.4.11); no secondary stress is described in the snippets seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifted from the penult to a preceding vowel by subsidiary rules (sec. 3.7.2: epenthetic e and the morpheme joiner -a- inserted after stress placement); rare words with final stress (one loan-like word 'unusual in that the final vowel is stressed', sec. 3.7.x); monosyllables extremely rare.
new_statements.identity_note: Bonvillain describes the Akwesasne (St. Regis) dialect of Mohawk; Potter's data are Mohawk without a dialect visible in the snippets (he cites G. Michelson 1973 A Thousand Words of Mohawk).

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate placement as the catalog's fixed-strict coding and as Bonvillain 1973 / Michelson 1988 held by the project; the full text adds: tonic lengthening in open stressed syllables, unstressable excrescent e (vs stressable epenthetic e), the stem-joiner -a- unstressed in an open penult (giving antepenultimate stress with lengthening) but stressed in a closed penult or after excrescent e, the disyllabic minimal word with prothetic i-, and stress 'correlated with a phonetic high tone'. These are the same lexical/derivational exceptions the catalog paraphrase already allows ('vowels may be inserted.. after stressing'), so no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (NonFinality >> Edgemost, moraic trochee), whether penult and final are open or closed; a stressed open syllable gets a long vowel. Vowels invisible or partly visible to stress produce surface antepenultimate stress: excrescent e (phonetic, never stressed, no lengthening, does not count for the disyllabic minimum) and the semantically empty joiner -a- (unstressed in an open penult, where stress and length go to the antepenult; stressed in a closed penult or when preceded by excrescent e); true epenthetic e is stressable. Underlyingly monosyllabic words get prothetic i- to satisfy a disyllabic minimum. Stress is correlated with phonetic high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described: the paper speaks only of the 'primary stressed syllable' and 'main foot'; no secondary stresses are marked or discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Excrescent e in the penult is skipped (te+k+rik+s -> tekeriks with antepenult stress); joiner -a- in an open penult is skipped with antepenult lengthening (tehsa?a:rarik), but stressed in a closed penult (kyntakwas) and in an open penult after excrescent e (Michelson 1988's exception); prothetic i- for monosyllables (k+ek+s -> i:keks).
new_statements.identity_note: Bonvillain describes the Akwesasne (St. Regis) dialect of Mohawk; Potter's data are Mohawk without a dialect visible in the snippets (he cites G. Michelson 1973 A Thousand Words of Mohawk).

tone_statements.quote: PMO also appears to have developed falling tone on penultimate vowels that were lengthened when they preceded a glottal consonant ( e.g. PNI * / kaˈnaɁtsjaɁ / 'pot, kettle' > PMO * / kaˈnâːtsjaɁ /; PNI * / oˈkahɹaɁ / 'eye' > PMO / oˈkâːɹaɁ / ). ... By PMO-7, an accented vowel has been lengthened and acquired falling tone when followed by a glottal stop or by * / h / plus a resonant consonant ( e.g. PNI * / niˈwaɁah / 'it is small' > PMO * / niˈwâːɁa /; PNI * / ohˈnjaɁsaɁ / 'neck' > PMO * / ohˈnjâːsaɁ / ... ). For some lexical exceptions to lengthening in this environment, see Michelson (1988:61-66).

tone_statements.quote: The diacritical marks used in writing the Mohawk language are: falling tone with length (Kawennénhtha tánon teiotsistóhkwake) (`:); rising tone with length (Kawennakará:tats tánon teiotsistóhkwake) (´:); rising tone stress (Kawennakára:tats) (´); glottal stop (Tekawénniaks) ('). ... The glottal stop alternates with length with falling tone. When stress is on the syllable, there is length with falling tone, as in kà:sere (car). When stress is not on a syllable, the glottal stop is used, as in ka'serehtí:io (nice car).

tone_statements.summary: Orthographic statement of the accent-bound tone system: the single stressed vowel of a word is written with acute (high/rising tone, short), acute+colon (rising tone, long) or grave+colon (falling tone, long); falling-tone length is the surface form of a stressed vowel plus following glottal stop, which resurfaces as ' when the stress shifts.

sources.note: Second-hand theoretical (OT) analysis of Mohawk stress and epenthesis, data from Michelson: stress is regularly penultimate, quantity-insensitive (penult and ultima open or closed), stressed open syllables lengthen, and excrescent (epenthetic) e in penult position is skipped. Hagstrom 1997 (held) quotes Potter 1994:354 for the hypothesis that the epenthetic vowel's mora is not dominated by a syllable node and only syllables are footed. Confirms the fixed-strict penult coding with the epenthesis caveat.

By PMO-7, an accented vowel has been lengthened and acquired falling tone when followed by a glottal stop or by * / h / plus a resonant consonant ( e.g. PNI * / niˈwaɁah / 'it is small' > PMO * / niˈwâːɁa /; PNI * / ohˈnjaɁsaɁ / 'neck' > PMO * / ohˈnjâːsaɁ / ... ). sources.quote: The diacritical marks used in writing the Mohawk language are: falling tone with length (Kawennénhtha tánon teiotsistóhkwake) (`:); rising tone with length (Kawennakará:tats tánon teiotsistóhkwake) (´:); rising tone stress (Kawennakára:tats) (´); glottal stop (Tekawénniaks) ('). ... The glottal stop alternates with length with falling tone. When stress is on the syllable, there is length with falling tone, as in kà:sere (car). When stress is not on a syllable, the glottal stop is used, as in ka'serehtí:io (nice car).

sources.note: The standard orthography writes three prosodic diacritics - falling tone with length (`:), rising tone with length (´:), rising tone stress (´) - plus apostrophe for glottal stop, and states the alternation: a stressed syllable with an underlying glottal stop surfaces as length with falling tone (kà:sere 'car'), the glottal stop reappearing when stress moves (ka'serehtí:io); diacritics for tone/length/stress introduced in 1972.

tone.quote: We can see that P codas usually count towards weight by considering their behavior in stressed syllables. Normally, when the syllable is stressed, the glottal stop deletes, with compensatory lengthening as well as a sharp falling tone on the vowel. This tone is not found elsewhere in the language. If such syllables counted as light in word-internal positions, we’d expect simple stress shift off of them.
